lessons.title: The Boss Arena: Containerize It!
lessons.content_md:
# The Boss Arena: Containerize It! ⚔️ You've learned about Data Centers, IaaS vs PaaS, Object Storage, and the power of Docker Containers. Now, it's time to prove you are ready to be a Cloud Engineer. In this final Capstone Project, you will write a real web application, package it perfectly into a Docker Container (the shipping container of the internet!), and push your code to GitHub. *(Our AI Capstone Evaluator will pull your GitHub repository and grade it — the last lesson of this level shows you how to submit.)* ## Step 1: The App 📄 Create a new folder on your computer called `cloud-capstone`. Inside that folder, create a file named `index.html`. Write the following code into the file: ```html My First Cloud App

Hello from the Cloud! ☁️

I have successfully containerized my first application.

``` ## Step 2: The Dockerfile 🐳 Now, we need to create the instructions to build our Docker container. We need a tiny, lightweight web server to serve our HTML file. In the exact same folder, create a file named `Dockerfile` (no extension). Write the following code: ```dockerfile # Use a lightweight Nginx web server image as our base FROM nginx:alpine # Copy our index.html file into the container's web directory COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html # Expose port 80 so the internet can see it EXPOSE 80 ``` ## Step 3: Build & Test (Optional) 🛠️ If you have Docker installed on your computer, you can build and test your container right now! Open your terminal and run: ```bash docker build -t my-cloud-app . docker run -p 8080:80 my-cloud-app ``` If you go to `http://localhost:8080` in your browser, you should see your app running perfectly inside its container! ## Step 4: Push to GitHub 🐙 To complete this level, you must push your code to a public GitHub repository. 1. Initialize a git repository: `git init` 2. Add your files: `git add index.html Dockerfile` 3. Commit: `git commit -m "My first containerized app"` 4. Push to a new public repo on your GitHub account. When you are done, click **Complete** to continue — next you'll plan your full capstone and submit it for grading.

lessons.title: Plan Your Cloud Capstone
lessons.content_md:
# Plan Your Cloud Capstone 🗺️

Your capstone should prove you can take an app and make it **cloud-ready**: containerised, configurable and easy for someone else to run.

## Pick a Scope You Can Finish

| Level | Project idea |
|-------|--------------|
| ✅ Core | A small web app or API in a Docker container, configured with environment variables |
| ⭐ Stronger | App + database with Docker Compose, plus a health-check endpoint |
| 🚀 Stand-out | Add a CI workflow, or Terraform that provisions the infrastructure |

Start with the core and add layers only when it works end to end.

## Follow the Twelve-Factor Basics

| Factor | In practice |
|--------|-------------|
| **Config in the environment** | Ports, database URLs and keys come from env vars, not code |
| **Dependencies declared** | `requirements.txt` / `package.json` pinned |
| **Stateless processes** | Store uploads and sessions in a database or bucket, not on the container's disk |
| **Logs to stdout** | Print logs; let the platform collect them |
| **Dev/prod parity** | The same container runs on your laptop and in the cloud |

<flipcard front="⚙️ Why keep config in environment variables?" back="The same container image can run in dev, staging and production with different settings — and secrets never end up in your code or image."></flipcard>

## Sketch the Architecture

Even a simple diagram in your README shows you understand the system:

```text
 User ──HTTPS──▶ Load balancer ──▶ [ web container ] ──▶ [ Postgres ]
                                         │
                                         └──▶ object storage (uploads)
```

## Plan Your Repository

```text
cloud-capstone/
├── README.md
├── Dockerfile
├── docker-compose.yml
├── .env.example          # variable names only, no real secrets
├── .dockerignore
├── app/                  # your application code
├── infra/                # optional: Terraform
└── .github/workflows/    # optional: CI
```

lessons.title: Ship It: Submission Checklist
lessons.content_md:
# Ship It: Submission Checklist 🚀

The **AI Capstone Evaluator** below reads your public GitHub repository and grades it out of 100. **60 or more passes** and completes the Cloud track — **+500 XP** and a shareable **certificate**. 🎓

## What the Reviewer Looks For

| Area | What earns points |
|------|-------------------|
| **Containerisation** | A working Dockerfile: small base image, layers cached sensibly, correct port |
| **Configuration** | Settings from environment variables; an `.env.example` |
| **Runs from a fresh clone** | Clear build and run commands in the README |
| **Cloud thinking** | Health check, logs to stdout, stateless design; Compose or IaC is a bonus |
| **Security** | No secrets committed; no unnecessary open ports |
| **Documentation** | What it is, how to run it, how it's put together |

## A Production-Minded Dockerfile

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt   # cached unless requirements change

COPY . .
RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser                                          # don't run as root

ENV PORT=8000
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["sh", "-c", "gunicorn -b 0.0.0.0:${PORT} app:app"]
```

## Final Checklist ✅

- [ ] Repository is **public** on GitHub
- [ ] `Dockerfile` builds and the container starts
- [ ] `README.md` has the `docker build` / `docker run` (or `docker compose up`) commands
- [ ] All configuration comes from environment variables, documented in `.env.example`
- [ ] **No secrets** in the repo — `.env` is in `.gitignore`
- [ ] A `.dockerignore` keeps `venv/`, `node_modules/` and `.git/` out of the image
- [ ] Optional: CI workflow or Terraform in `infra/`

<flipcard front="🐳 Why add a .dockerignore?" back="It stops large or sensitive folders (venv, node_modules, .git, .env) from being sent to the Docker build — smaller, faster and safer images."></flipcard>

## Submit 👇

Paste your repository URL into the evaluator below. If you don't pass the first time, use the feedback to improve and resubmit — your best attempt counts.
